This paper is arranged in three sections, A, B and C. Section A: answer ALL 5 questions; you will be graded for the best 4 answers. Section B: answer ALL TWO questions in this section. Section C: answer 2 questions out of 3; if you attempt more than 2 questions, only the first 2 will be considered. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators are allowed. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown: Using different examples, describe how each of these factors (temperature, concentration, surface area and catalyst) affect the rate of chemical reactions.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Basic idea (collision theory).** A reaction happens when reacting particles collide with at least a minimum energy (the activation energy). The rate of reaction is the change in the amount (or concentration) of a reactant or product per unit time. Each factor changes either how often particles collide or how many collisions are successful.

**1. Temperature**

Raising the temperature **increases the rate**. The particles move faster and have more energy, so they collide more often and, above all, a much larger fraction of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. As a rough rule, the rate doubles for every $10\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ rise.

*Example:* sodium thiosulphate and dilute hydrochloric acid, $\mathrm{Na_2S_2O_3} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{SO_2} + \mathrm{S}$. The yellow sulphur makes the mixture cloudy and hides a cross drawn under the flask. At $50\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the cross disappears much sooner than at $20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. (Food also goes bad more slowly in a refrigerator.)

**2. Concentration**

Increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution (or the pressure of a gas) **increases the rate**. More particles per unit volume means that collisions occur more frequently.

*Example:* magnesium ribbon with hydrochloric acid, $\mathrm{Mg} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_2} + \mathrm{H_2}$. With $2\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ acid, hydrogen bubbles off much faster (the volume of gas collected in a given time is greater, the ribbon disappears sooner) than with $0.5\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ acid. The final volume of hydrogen is the same because the amount of magnesium is the same.

**3. Surface area (particle size) of a solid**

Breaking a solid into smaller pieces **increases the rate**. Only the particles at the surface can collide with the other reactant, so a larger exposed surface gives more collisions per second.

*Example:* calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid, $\mathrm{CaCO_3} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCl_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{CO_2}$. Powdered marble gives carbon dioxide much faster than the same mass of marble chips. (Flour or coal dust in the air burns explosively for the same reason.)

**4. Catalyst**

A catalyst **increases the rate** by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions are successful. It is not used up and is chemically unchanged at the end; it does not change the amount of product formed.

*Example:* decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, $2\mathrm{H_2O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{O_2}$. Without a catalyst the reaction is very slow; when manganese(IV) oxide, $\mathrm{MnO_2}$, is added, oxygen is evolved rapidly (a glowing splint relights), and the $\mathrm{MnO_2}$ can be filtered off and weighed unchanged. Industrial examples: iron in the Haber process, $\mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3}$, and vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process, $2\mathrm{SO_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO_3}$.
